title: New research sheds light on frozen mummies of the Andes | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Three children ages 6, 8 and 14 took an arduous, perhaps monthslong journey about 500 years ago to the roughly 20,600-foot (6,300-meter)summit of Mount Ampato, a sacred Inca site high up in the Andes.

They didn’t make it back down — but it wasn’t the climb that caused their untimely deaths.

Dozens of other children and young women who made treks todifferentAndean peaks met similar fates. All were killed as human sacrifices as part of a ritual known ascapacochathat took place across the Inca Empire during the 15th and 16th centuries. But a string of new evidence suggests these individuals’ final moments were stranger and more varied than previously imagined.

Some of their bodies, mostly discovered in the 1990s in what’s nowPeru, Chile and Argentina, were so immaculately preserved by the cold, dry, high-altitude conditions that they looked asleep. Their lifelike state makes these so-called “ice mummies” rewarding for scientists to study, but what happened to these children, particularly in physical terms, still isn’t fully understood.

New research published over the course of 2026, including medical scans and forensic and chemical analysis of the ice mummies’ hair and nails, is adding detail to the children’s stories, revealing how they were killed, the drugs used during their sacrifices and the long journey that preceded their deaths.

“These frozen mummies are as close to real time capsules as you can get,” said Johan Reinhard, an anthropologist and National Geographic explorer-in-residence who discovered the first frozen mummy on Mount Ampato in 1995: the 14-year-old girl known asthe Ice Maiden or Juanita. He went on to find two more mummified children on the same mountain that year.

Between 1996 and 1999, he discovered 15 more mummies on mountains in the Andes above 18,044 feet (5,500 meters).

In his 1995 expedition, Reinhard had climbed the north face of Ampato — a peak taller than Mount McKinley and Mont Blanc — to take pictures of the eruption of anearby volcano.That’s when he and his climbing partner saw a bundle in an ice-filled crater that appeared to have fallen from a platform on a ridge near the summit. From afar, it looked like a climber’s backpack, but when he and his climbing partner turned it over and saw a face poking through the cloth, they quickly realized its importance. They transported the surprisingly heavy mummy on donkeys and a bus,racing to get it down the mountain to the nearest city with a freezer before it thawed.

“We were wrapping it, insulating it with the pads we slept on,” he recalled, “so we could protect the mummy.”

Children and young women were sacrificed throughout theInca Empire, which began in the 13th century and ended in 1572 with the Spanish conquest, as an act of veneration for important deities. In death, the chosen became intermediaries between the living and the divine.

Much of the knowledge about the ritual comes from chronicles written by Spanish colonizers. These accounts suggested only children of exceptional beauty were selected to be sacrificed in what was believed to be an honor for their families, although scholars disagree over the selection progress. The Incas had no written language, but some records were kept using knotted string or cord known as quipu.

“We don’t have any direct information from people who actually saw the ritual,” said Dagmara Socha, an archaeologist in the Center for Andean Studies at Poland’s University of Warsaw, who has been involved in much of the recent research. “All of it is secondhand so some things could be misunderstood,” she said referring to the Spaniards’ chronicles. This lack of first-person accounts makes the mummies particularly important, she added.

The chosen children were often taken to the imperial capital of Cuzco, where they participated in elaborate ceremonies before being sent to sacred sites in all corners of the empire, she explained. These processions could take months, traversing vast distances and difficult terrain before reaching the high-altitude sacrificial sites.

Socha led the toxicological analysis of hair and nail samples from eight child mummies — seven girls and one boy — found bundled in textiles atop five mountains in Peru and Argentina, including two of those found by Reinard on Mount Ampato. The work, published this monthin thejournal Antiquity, confirmed that the children were plied with a variety of drugs in the months to weeks before they died — possibly to ease the ordeal ahead.

In all eight of the mummies, researchers found traces of cocaine, suggesting the children consumed coca leaves, which naturally contain the substance. This practice was a deeply embedded part of Inca culture and ritual that may have helped to reduce altitude sickness and fatigue during the journey preceding their deaths.

New technological advances could detect even low concentrations of psychoactive drugs in centuries-old samples of keratin, a protein in hair and nails that preserves chemical traces of substances consumed in life, Socha said.

In four of the mummies, the scientists found evidence of alcohol consumption, most likely chicha beer made from maize. The Incas gave these children chicha to dull their senses and keep them calm, according to the Spanish chronicles.

Earlier research on a hair sample failed to detect psychoactive substances. But in the new analysis, one hair sample, belonging to an 8-year-old Inca girl found on a shrine on top of Mount Chuscha in northwestern Argentina, revealed how levels of cocaine and alcohol varied over the six months before her death, suggesting that the children were drugged much earlier before their final days and hours.

Socha said the most intriguing finding was detecting traces of the chemical harmine in the famous ice mummy that Reinhard found on Mount Ampato in southern Peru in 1995. The chemical compound comes from one of two plants traditionally used inayahuasca, a hallucinogenic brew still used today, although Socha said it wasn’t clear if the girl was given the substance to induce hallucinations. Used alone, the study said harmine had antidepressant properties.

More likely, the new findings suggest the children received concoctions that would have enhanced their well-being and mood given that these hallucinogenic drugs could be potentially lethal.

“We have information from the chronicles that the important thing was the attitude of the children — they needed to go happy to the gods,” Socha said.

“This mountain terrain is very rough,” said Socha, who has made the journey to some of the mountain sitesfor her field work. “I suffer for myself, and I can imagine how it could be for the children to travel in this difficult terrain at this high altitude.”

Fresh analysis of other remains of children who died in these rituals offer additional clues. Verónica Silva-Pinto, a curator of bioanthropology at the National Museum of Natural History of Chile, and her colleagues revisited three mummies from two capacocha sacrificial sites inresearch published in Julyin the journal Science Advances.

These included the “Niño de El Plomo” or El Plomo Boy, who was about age 8 or 9 in the 15th century when he was killed near the 17,700-foot (5,400-meter) summit of El Plomo, now in central Chile; and two girls, one about age 9 and the other about 18, who were sacrificed about 30 years earlier near the top of Cerro Esmeralda in northern Chile’s Atacama Desert.

Archaeologists thought the girls were strangled, and signs of frostbite on the boy’s fingers led them to believe he froze to death. However, newly conducted CT scans found they died in different ways than initially thought.

The marks on the girls’ necks could have been caused by the textiles their bodies were wrapped in after death and were likely not the result of a ligature that would indicate strangulation, the study in Science Advances found, while the boy’s skull showed evidence of blunt force trauma.

“With the help of two engineers, we compared the different strengths and different tools that could cause that wound,” said Silva-Pinto, who is also a scholar at Chile’s Universidad Diego Portales. “With that information we reached the conclusion of which weapon caused the blow.”

Specifically, the pattern of damage suggested the boy had been clubbed to death with an Inca mace that had a distinctive star-shaped head. It’s not clear how the girls died, she added.

The scan also revealed that the boy’s stomach was full at the time of his death, which was consistent with a final ceremonial meal. Not long afterward, he vomited, according to the study — evidenced by a dilated esophagus and stains on his clothing. Vomiting could be a reaction triggered by the final blow to his skull, Silva-Pinto said.

Separate CT scans that Socha and her colleagues performed on the ice mummies, including Juanita the famous Ice Maiden, found on Ampato, and one other mountain, also showed the children’s digestive tracts were full.

The imaging,published in a study earlier this year,confirmed that Juanita had trauma to the skull, chest and pelvis, indicating a violent cause of death. The finding verifies information from an unpublished scan conducted at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1996 when the mummy briefly went on public display in the United States that year.

The study also revealed that a fourth ice mummy found on Ampato in 1997 likely wasn’t killed there: The bones weren’t in their correct anatomical position; some were missing and the abdominal cavity had been stuffed with textiles unlike the other mummies, which were intact.

“It could be that when people moved,” Socha said, “they took sacred things with them and buried them in the new location to have contact with the local gods and reestablish connection with the sacred landscape.”

Using a technique known as stable isotope analysis, Silva-Pinto also studied chemical traces of nitrogen in the children’s braided hair that suggested their diet had changed dramatically and repeatedly in the months before their deaths. This change in diet, she said, reflected the prolonged ritual passage the children made to the sacrifice site.

The El Plomo Boy undertook the longest journey, she said, traveling more than 1,615 miles (2,600 kilometers) over nine months; the shift in his diet likely occurred along the way as local communities received the procession and offered the child and his attendants food. A buildup of thick, hardened skin on his feet — unusual for a child his age — was evidence of the extended trek, according to the Science Advances study.

Analysis of botanical remains found alongside a mummy discovered in 1999 during a dig led by Reinhard atop Mount Llullaillaco has given some insight into the probable reasons Inca leaders chose to sacrifice children—which included political motivations.The girl, age 14 at the time of death, is perhaps the best preserved and most lifelike of all the mummies, Socha said.

Previous radiocarbon dating placed the burial between 1430 and 1520. However, new dates for maize, coca leaves and manioc seeds — or cassava seeds — found with the girl, which probably came from plants harvested the same year or year before the ritual sacrifice, narrowed the time frame to between 1462 and 1507, accordingto a study published in June.

The point in time coincided with the reign of two major Inca rulers, Topa Inca and Huayna Capac, who presided over a southward expansion of the empire. This historical context, Socha reasoned, suggested a political rationale for the sacrifice at Llullaillaco, which may have served to anchor the Inca presence in the region, rather than a sacrifice related to a natural event such as a volcanic eruption.

At 22,109 feet (6,739 meters), Llullaillaco is the world’shighest archaeological site. Unlike some of the others, the mummified individuals found on this peak aren’t believed to have met violent deaths, Socha said. Perhaps they succumbed to the extreme cold while drugged and unconscious either before or after they were placed in their burial site.

Socha and Silva-Pinto said there are more chapters to add to the ice mummies’ stories. Initial studies of the children’s DNA were completed more than a decade ago, revealing their sex and other details. But advancing forensic and chemical techniques have allowed researchers to sequence the full genome of some of the mummies. This new research is due to publish in coming months and could shed light on the children’s origins and health, the two scientists said.

Reinhard, who is almost 83, said he didn’t immediately realize to what extent the ice mummies would captivate the world. Nor did he anticipate the variety and quantity of studies that would later be conducted on the children.

“A frozen mummy never stops giving new information,” he said.
